questions.q: What problem does a feature store specifically solve among the six components?
options: Logging training run parameters for later comparison
Ensuring the same feature definition is used consistently in both training and live prediction
Scheduling data prep and training as a reproducible job
Packaging a trained model for rollout
questions.explain: A feature store's job is defining, storing, and serving input features so training and production prediction use the exact same definition — not logging runs, scheduling jobs, or packaging models.

questions.q: Why is versioning and lineage described as a 'thread' rather than a standalone component?
options: Because it only applies to the model registry
Because it is optional and only needed for regulated industries
Because every other component — feature store, pipeline, registry, deployment — needs to answer which version ran, on what data, producing what result
Because it replaces the need for a feature store
questions.explain: Versioning and lineage runs through all the other components rather than standing alone, since each one needs traceability back to a specific version and a specific run.

questions.q: In the model lifecycle walkthrough, what typically happens right after a pipeline trains a candidate model?
options: The model is immediately served to all production traffic with no further steps
The run's parameters, metrics, and artifacts are logged to the experiment tracker
The feature store is deleted and rebuilt
Monitoring immediately triggers a rollback
questions.explain: After a pipeline trains a candidate, the run is logged to the experiment tracker so it can be compared against other runs before any promotion or deployment decision is made.

questions.q: What does a model registry track that a pipeline orchestrator does not?
options: Which stage a specific model version is in — staging, production, or archived
The schedule for running data prep jobs
Live prediction latency
Feature backfill history
questions.explain: The model registry is a versioned catalog tracking lifecycle stage (staging, production, archived) for trained models — a distinct job from the pipeline orchestrator, which schedules and sequences jobs.

questions.q: Why do the same six component names show up whether a company uses one managed platform or a fully self-hosted open-source stack?
options: Because every company is legally required to use identical tool names
Because the six underlying jobs map onto the stages every supervised ML project goes through, regardless of which tools implement them
Because open-source and managed platforms are technically the same codebase
Because monitoring is not actually needed on managed platforms
questions.explain: The six components map almost one-to-one onto universal ML project stages — getting data ready, experimenting, picking a winner, shipping it, watching it — so the jobs are consistent even when the specific tools differ.
